newsitem.title: MEXICO: FOCUS - Mexico unveils $6 bln debt refinancing.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Mexico unveils $6 bln debt refinancing.

text.p: Mexico on Tuesday unveiled plans to refinance a whopping $6 billion in loans it had raised to pay off the U.S. government, saying it would no longer pledge oil revenues as a guarantee against default.

In a surprise move that government officials said would cut debt service costs and ease amortization pressure in the last three years of the current administration, the Finance Ministry also announced a slew of new and planned bond issues worth more than $4 billion.

Analysts said the main blessing was that the operation would prematurely pay off a five-year floating-rate note issued in August last year that was guaranteed -- to the bane of many Mexicans -- with oil revenues by Petroleos Mexicanos (Pemex).

The possibility that foreign bondholders could, if Mexico ever defaulted, have first claim on Mexico's oil wealth was always a painful one in a staunchly nationalistic country. Also, investors prefer plain bond issues because the value of collateral is hard to measure.
"It liberates Pemex payments and saves them money -- that's good news," said Enrique Ramirez, an economist at Santander Investments in Mexico City.
The $6 billion was raised last year to help Mexico repay an emergency U.S. Treasury loan issued in 1995 when the country was on the verge of financial collapse.

It was supposed to last for five years, but market conditions have improved for Mexico since, enabling it to raise money on better terms despite the fact that the previous loan had a better credit rating because of the oil collateral.

"It's a big advantage," Alejandro Valenzuela, spokesman at the Finance Ministry, told Reuters. "If you look at the average maturities that we're obtaining we're going from 2-1/2 years to almost seven years."
"Also, the mix of resources we're obtaining is actually a little bit better in spite of the fact that the other one had a better (credit) rating."

Savings in terms of interest payments are an unspectacular $25 million a year, but the average annual amortization bill to the end of the millenium shrank to $935 million -- a manageable sum, analysts said.

Raising $6 billion is no easy task for any country, but Mexico, which just 2-1/2 years ago crushed foreign investors with a devastating devaluation, has taken tapping the markets to a virtual art form.

So far this year it has raised $2.5 billion on international markets in Japan, Italy and Britain, which it has quietly stashed in its coffers in preparation for the prepayment. Part of that was $930 million in hitherto unnanounced short-term bridge loans, Valenzuela said.
The Finance Ministry said on Tuesday it completed three new bond market operations, raising $2 billion:

-- In one it found an additional $500 million by increasing the amount of a $1 billion 10-year global issued in January -- saving money in the process because the enhanced issue did not need to be re-registered with the Securities and Exchange Commission.

Market sources said the increased size of the issue was aimed at staving off a short squeeze in the paper, as well as raising money. One of the main holders of the bond had been Inbursa, owned by savvy Mexican trader Carlos Slim. He recently sold much of that stake, and market players speculated he probably made a big profit.
-- In another operation, it sold a $1 billion five-year floating-rate note.
-- It also wrapped up a $500 million medium-term note program.
The Finance Ministry announced another $1.5 billion in bond deals due to be completed shortly, including the floating of $1.1 billion in medium-term notes chiefly in Europe.
